name: KeyboardKit / KeyboardKit Pro (iOS)
important_status_correction: The task brief describes the 9.x state ('KeyboardStyleService is deprecated in favor of view-modifier-based styling'). As of this research the shipping line is KeyboardKit 10.x (10.7.3, released July 2026) - the services were SOFT-DEPRECATED in 9.8 and REMOVED in 10.0. So view-modifier styling is no longer merely 'the current correct shape', it is the ONLY shape; any 9.x tutorial showing a custom KeyboardStyleService subclass is now dead code. Design against modifiers + KeyboardTheme, not services.
primary_sources: https://github.com/KeyboardKit/KeyboardKitPro (Pro - closed-source binary distribution, but public RELEASE_NOTES.md and issue tracker)
rendering_approach: PER-KEY styling with an optional whole-surface background - i.e. hybrid, but assembled very differently from the Android references because there is no Drawable/Canvas layer at all. Every key is a SwiftUI view (`Keyboard.Button`) that receives a `Keyboard.ButtonStyle` value; the theme supplies those styles as data rather than as art. A `KeyboardTheme` carries `buttonStyles: [ButtonType: Keyboard.ButtonStyle]`, so styling is per-ROLE (input / system / primary) rather than per-key-instance, plus a `buttonPressedOverlayColor: Color?` for the pressed state. Behind the keys sits `backgroundStyle: Keyboard.Background?`, a layered background value applied to the whole keyboard view. There is NO per-key bitmap/9-patch mechanism comparable to FUTO's KeyBackground - key 'art' on iOS is expressed as corner radius, border color/size, shadow color/size, background color and foreground color, i.e. vector-ish style properties rather than supplied images. A theme CAN put an image behind the keys (see compositing_scrim_model) but cannot put a distinct image ON a key. That is the single biggest expressiveness gap versus FUTO if your design calls for illustrated key caps.
rendering_pipeline: Pure SwiftUI, which is both the framework's reason to exist and the source of its constraints. The keyboard extension's `KeyboardInputViewController` hosts a SwiftUI hierarchy rooted at `KeyboardView`; keys are `Keyboard.Button` views; `Keyboard.Background` itself conforms to `View` (`@MainActor struct Background: Decodable, Encodable, Equatable, Sendable, View`) so the background is composited by SwiftUI's own layering rather than by manual drawing. Styling flows through the SwiftUI ENVIRONMENT via view modifiers, so re-styling is a normal SwiftUI invalidation. Per-keystroke cost: a keypress mutates observable state (KeyboardContext etc.) and SwiftUI re-renders the affected buttons - materially different from the Android references, where a keypress is a cheap Canvas invalidate. This is the one place where an iOS SwiftUI keyboard can go wrong: over-broad observable state causes the whole keyboard to re-render per keystroke, and the framework's move from services to value builders + `@MainActor` annotations is partly about making that cost predictable. There is no UIKit/CALayer fallback path for key drawing. The iOS analogue of the Android 'Compose lifecycle owners inside InputMethodService' blocker does not exist - SwiftUI inside a keyboard extension is a supported configuration - but the ~40-60MB extension memory ceiling replaces it as the dominant platform constraint (see memory_performance_budget). [uncertain] - I found no published per-keystroke render benchmarks from the project.
compositing_scrim_model:
This is KeyboardKit's strongest and most directly copyable piece for background-image theming: `Keyboard.Background` is an explicitly LAYERED value type, documented as 'optional layered rendering from bottom to top', with a single initializer exposing every layer at once:

  init(backgroundColor: Color?,
       backgroundGradient: [Color]?,
       imageData: Data?,
       imageContentMode: ImageContentMode,
       overlayColor: Color?,
       overlayGradient: [Color]?)

Stack, bottom to top: backgroundColor -> backgroundGradient -> image (from raw `Data`, laid out per `imageContentMode`) -> overlayColor -> overlayGradient -> then the key layer above it. The `overlayColor` / `overlayGradient` pair IS the scrim, and making it a first-class field of the background value - rather than something folded into key alpha (FUTO) or left to the author (HeliBoard) - is the cleanest of the three models. It also means a scrim is serializable, since the whole struct is Codable. Convenience factories exist for the common cases: `.color(_:)`, `.verticalGradient(_:)`, `.image(_:contentMode:)`, `.image(data:contentMode:)`, `.image(systemName:contentMode:)`, plus a `.standard` default. There are also `topAccessoryBackgroundColor` and `bottomAccessoryBackgroundColor` view properties for the areas above/below the keyboard proper. NO BLUR field exists in the background value - a blurred background must be pre-blurred in the image or achieved with a SwiftUI `.blur()`/material outside the theme model, which is a real gap versus FUTO's shader path. Note also the documented iOS quirk that KeyboardKit works around: semi-transparent colors are used to route around a system bug affecting keyboard-extension color rendering - relevant if you implement transparency yourself.
asset_types: Raster images carried as raw `Data` inside the style value - `Keyboard.Background.imageData: Data?` - which is the defining choice of this model: there is no filename, no path, no bundle reference and no asset catalog lookup in a theme. The image travels INSIDE the Codable struct, so a theme is genuinely self-contained (see theme_package_manifest_format) at the cost of base64/Data bloat. `ImageContentMode` (a nested Codable enum) controls fit/fill behavior. Alongside that, the framework provides vector SF Symbols and its own bundled `Image` assets for key glyphs, exposed as builders - `Image.keyboardCase`, `Image.keyboardType`, plus arrow/escape/function/space/URL-domain icons added in 10.7.0 - and a `KeyboardFont` type for typography. KeyboardKit Pro adds VECTORIZED emoji-specific assets (`.keyboardEmoji`, `.emojiCategory(_:)`), which matters because emoji-panel category icons are a surface most theme systems forget. Density bucketing is not a concern on iOS in the Android sense - SF Symbols and SwiftUI shapes are resolution-independent, and only the user's background photo is resolution-bound. No 9-patch concept exists or is needed, since key 'art' is corner-radius + border + shadow rather than a stretched bitmap. No Lottie, no GIF, no video, no shaders in the theme model.
theme_package_manifest_format:
There is no zip, no manifest FILE and no on-disk theme package format at all - and that is a legitimate design, not an omission. A theme is a CODABLE SWIFT VALUE: `KeyboardTheme` declares `init(from:)` (Decodable) and its constituent style types are Codable too (`Keyboard.Background` is `Decodable, Encodable, Equatable, Sendable, View`; there is a dedicated `Color+Codable.swift` in Sources/KeyboardKit/Styling to make SwiftUI `Color` round-trip). So the serialization format is 'whatever you encode it to' - JSONEncoder output is the natural choice - and because `imageData: Data?` is embedded, a single encoded blob carries the background IMAGE as well as the colors. That is a real advantage over HeliBoard (whose shared theme silently omits the background image) and a different tradeoff from FUTO (zip with separate asset entries and lazy on-demand decoding). Theme fields, from the docs:

  id: UUID
  name: String
  collectionName: String
  author: Author?
  backgroundStyle: Keyboard.Background?
  foregroundColor: Color?
  buttonStyles: [ButtonType: Keyboard.ButtonStyle]
  buttonPressedOverlayColor: Color?
  autocompleteToolbarStyle: AutocompleteToolbarStyle?
  calloutStyle: KeyboardCalloutStyle?
  emojiKeyboardStyle: EmojiKeyboardStyle
  keyboardViewStyle: KeyboardViewStyle?
  isPredefined: Bool

Note `collectionName` and `author` - the model anticipates theme collections and attribution, i.e. it was designed with a catalog in mind. There is a convenience initializer taking RAW style properties instead of composed style structs, which is the practical authoring path (see token_count_tiering).
token_count_tiering: Two tiers, expressed as two initializers on the same struct rather than as two file formats - an elegant alternative to HeliBoard's tier-dependent serialization. SIMPLE/RAW tier: `init(id:name:collectionName:author:backgroundStyle:foregroundColor:inputForegroundColor:inputBackgroundColor:systemForegroundColor:systemBackgroundColor:primaryForegroundColor:primaryBackgroundColor:buttonCornerRadius:buttonBorderColor:buttonBorderSize:buttonPressedOverlayColor:buttonShadowColor:buttonShadowSize:calloutForegroundColor:calloutBackgroundColor:calloutSelectedForegroundColor:calloutSelectedBackgroundColor:calloutSelectedCornerRadius:autocompleteForegroundColor:autocorrectForegroundColor:autocorrectBackgroundColor:autocorrectBackgroundCornerRadius:)` - roughly 26 flat parameters, of which ~19 are visual tokens (6 fg/bg color pairs across input/system/primary roles, 4 callout tokens, 3 autocomplete tokens, plus corner radius, border color/size, shadow color/size, pressed overlay). ADVANCED tier: `init(id:name:collectionName:author:backgroundStyle:foregroundColor:buttonStyles:buttonPressedOverlayColor:autocompleteToolbarStyle:calloutStyle:)` - you compose full style structs yourself, and `buttonStyles: [ButtonType: Keyboard.ButtonStyle]` plus `emojiKeyboardStyle` and `keyboardViewStyle` open up considerably more surface. So: ~19-26 named tokens at the simple tier, effectively unbounded at the composed tier. That sits between HeliBoard's 7/10/41 and FUTO's 44 + unbounded match rules. A third axis is `KeyboardThemeStyleVariation` / the `KeyboardThemeCopyable` protocol - a theme can be COPIED AND TWEAKED into named variations (which is how Colorful ships 8 color options and Tron 6 from one base), so the shipped catalog is far larger than the number of hand-authored themes.
theme_versioning_forward_compat: No explicit schema-version field on `KeyboardTheme`, and no documented migration mechanism - forward compatibility is delegated entirely to Swift `Codable` semantics, which is the weakest versioning story of the three items. Practical consequences: most style fields are OPTIONAL (`backgroundStyle: Keyboard.Background?`, `foregroundColor: Color?`, `calloutStyle: KeyboardCalloutStyle?`, `autocompleteToolbarStyle: AutocompleteToolbarStyle?`, `keyboardViewStyle: KeyboardViewStyle?`), so a decoder tolerates their absence and adding new optional properties will not break previously-encoded themes - but adding a NON-optional property, or renaming/retyping one, breaks decoding outright unless custom CodingKeys and a migration are written by hand. Unknown extra keys are ignored by the default synthesized decoder. Because the format is 'a Swift type', the FRAMEWORK VERSION is the de facto schema version, and the 9.x -> 10.x transition is a live example of that being disruptive: services were soft-deprecated in 9.8 and removed in 10.0. If you persist encoded themes (as `KeyboardThemeContext.settings` does), you own the migration when the struct changes - so stamp your own version field into whatever envelope you persist rather than relying on Codable alone. [uncertain] - I found no published statement about theme-decoding stability across major versions or any first-party migration helper.
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Fully PRE-BAKED - and this is a hard platform difference to plan around, not a framework shortcoming. iOS gives a keyboard extension no wallpaper-color API, so there is no Material You / Android 12+ dynamic-color analogue and no Palette-style extraction from an image anywhere in KeyboardKit; every color in a theme is a literal value the author chose. What the framework provides instead: standard adaptive colors via a keyboard-specific `Color` extension set (`Color+Keyboard.swift`) that follow light/dark appearance automatically, standard per-action colors and fonts (`KeyboardAction+ButtonColor.swift`, `+ButtonFont.swift`, `+ButtonImage.swift`, `+ButtonText.swift`, `+ButtonStyle.swift`), and standard builders reachable as `KeyboardAction.standardButtonImage(for: context)` / `.standardButtonText(for: context)` so your custom builder can fall back to system-correct values for the cases you don't override. Light/dark adaptation is therefore automatic for STANDARD styles but must be authored explicitly for a custom theme - a theme is one palette, and if you want day/night variants you ship two themes (or two style variations) and switch them, unlike HeliBoard's built-in PREF_THEME_COLORS/_NIGHT pair. There is also a documented workaround where semi-transparent colors are used to route around a system color bug in keyboard extensions. `Color+Random.swift` exists for generating palettes but is a development convenience, not extraction.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: No automatic validation - no WCAG ratio check, no APCA, and no luminance-delta guard comparable to FUTO's 0.08 minimum. Nothing in the theme model measures a foreground color against the composited background, and because the background can include an arbitrary user image plus optional overlay gradients, a correct check would have to sample the composited result rather than compare two color values - and no such sampling exists. Legibility is left to the theme author. Mitigations that DO exist: the `overlayColor` / `overlayGradient` layers give an author a first-class, serializable scrim to darken a photo deliberately (better tooling for the job than either Android reference, even though it is not enforced); `buttonBorderColor` / `buttonBorderSize` provide a key-border escape hatch equivalent to HeliBoard's borders toggle; `buttonShadowColor` / `buttonShadowSize` add separation from busy backgrounds; `foregroundColor` and per-role foreground colors are independently settable so labels can be lifted off any background. Release 10.5.0 increased FONT WEIGHTS for images and lowercase text specifically 'to enhance visual clarity', and the docs note KeyboardTheme adjustments made for readability - so accessibility work happens at the FRAMEWORK-DEFAULT level, not as author-facing enforcement. Standard SwiftUI/UIKit accessibility (Dynamic Type, Bold Text, Increase Contrast) applies to the hosting views but is not wired into theme color selection. [uncertain] - no evidence of any contrast API or lint in the public docs.
background_geometry_adaptation: Handled by SwiftUI layout plus one explicit knob, and it is the right primitive but a thin one. `Keyboard.Background.imageContentMode: ImageContentMode` (a Codable nested enum) is the single control - fit vs fill semantics, mapping onto SwiftUI's `ContentMode`. Because the background is itself a SwiftUI `View` composited into the keyboard's frame, it re-lays-out automatically for: portrait/landscape rotation, the different keyboard heights iOS uses per orientation and device, iPad vs iPhone, and the floating iPad keyboard - no per-orientation asset is needed, in contrast to HeliBoard which had to add separate portrait/landscape images. `topAccessoryBackgroundColor` and `bottomAccessoryBackgroundColor` cover the strips above/below the key area so the background doesn't end abruptly. What is MISSING relative to FUTO: there is no normalized crop rect and no focal-point/gravity control, so with `.fill` the framework decides what gets cropped and an author cannot say 'always keep this region visible'. On a keyboard, whose aspect ratio swings hard between iPhone portrait (very wide, short) and iPad landscape, that is a genuine limitation - a face or logo can be cropped out at one geometry and centered at another. If you are designing a theme format, take FUTO's fractional `cropping = [x0,y0,x1,y1]` and add it alongside a content mode. Split keyboard on iPad: [uncertain] - not documented in the sources I reached.
layout_locale_independence: Strong, for the same structural reason as HeliBoard: nothing in the theme model is positional. `buttonStyles` is keyed by `ButtonType` (input / system / primary) and the runtime builder discriminates on `KeyboardAction`, so a theme never references a row index, a column, or a key count. It therefore survives: different locale layouts (KeyboardKit Pro ships a large set of localized keyboards - QWERTY/AZERTY/QWERTZ and many non-Latin scripts), RTL languages, iPhone vs iPad layouts (which differ substantially in key count and in which keys exist at all), the numeric/symbolic keyboard types, and the emoji keyboard - the last of which gets its own `emojiKeyboardStyle` slot so it does not have to be forced through the key vocabulary. Because targeting is by `KeyboardAction` rather than by glyph position, a rule like 'style the primary/return key' correctly follows that key wherever the layout puts it, and `KeyboardReturnKeyType` handling means it also adapts when the host app changes it from Return to Search to Go. The one thing a theme CANNOT do - decorate one specific key differently by position - is also the thing that would have broken under layout changes, so the constraint and the robustness are the same fact. Background art independence is separate and weaker: with `.fill` and no crop rect, art can shift under layout-driven aspect changes (see background_geometry_adaptation).
non_key_surface_coverage: Good, and explicitly enumerated in the theme struct rather than left implicit - each major non-key surface gets a dedicated slot. Covered: the AUTOCOMPLETE/SUGGESTION TOOLBAR (`autocompleteToolbarStyle: AutocompleteToolbarStyle?`, with the raw-property initializer additionally exposing `autocompleteForegroundColor`, `autocorrectForegroundColor`, `autocorrectBackgroundColor`, `autocorrectBackgroundCornerRadius` - so the autocorrect 'chip' is themed separately from ordinary suggestions); CALLOUTS, i.e. both the key-preview bubble and the long-press action callout (`calloutStyle: KeyboardCalloutStyle?`, plus `calloutForegroundColor`, `calloutBackgroundColor`, `calloutSelectedForegroundColor`, `calloutSelectedBackgroundColor`, `calloutSelectedCornerRadius` - note selected-vs-unselected callout items are distinct tokens, finer-grained than either Android reference); the EMOJI KEYBOARD (`emojiKeyboardStyle: EmojiKeyboardStyle`, with Pro adding vectorized category assets `.keyboardEmoji` / `.emojiCategory(_:)`); the overall KEYBOARD VIEW (`keyboardViewStyle: KeyboardViewStyle?`, applied via `.keyboardViewStyle(_:)`); and the accessory strips above/below via `topAccessoryBackgroundColor` / `bottomAccessoryBackgroundColor`. NOT applicable on iOS: system navigation bar color (no such surface for an extension) - so HeliBoard's NAVIGATION_BAR has no counterpart. [uncertain] - dictation UI, and any clipboard/settings sheets a host app builds, are Pro/app-level surfaces whose theming coverage I could not confirm from the public docs.
sound_haptic_theming: Present and swappable, though as a SEPARATE namespace from theming rather than as part of a `KeyboardTheme` - the same split FUTO and HeliBoard make, but with far better first-party support. `KeyboardFeedback` is its own namespace containing feedback types and views, an OBSERVABLE CONTEXT and AUTO-PERSISTED SETTINGS, plus services that trigger feedback - structurally parallel to `KeyboardThemeContext`. An `AudioFeedback` enum wraps system sounds and, critically, supports a `.customUrl` case for playing URL-based sound effects from custom audio files, which makes actual SOUND PACKS feasible - the only item in this survey where that is true. A `HapticFeedback` enum wraps native types (selection changed, error, success, etc.). Since 8.5 you can REGISTER custom audio and haptic feedback for any gesture on any action and the standard action handler triggers it, with no action-handler subclassing required - the same 'register a value, don't subclass a service' philosophy as the styling migration. Underlying platform APIs are AudioToolbox system sounds / AVFoundation for custom URLs and UIFeedbackGenerator-family haptics. [uncertain] - whether custom audio requires Full Access to read a file from an App Group container is not stated in the sources I reached; bundling the sound inside the extension avoids the question entirely.
platform_apis_frameworks: iOS/iPadOS (with some macOS/visionOS/watchOS reach in recent versions), Swift + SwiftUI throughout. Core platform pieces: `UIInputViewController` subclassed as `KeyboardInputViewController`; `UITextDocumentProxy` for text interaction; SwiftUI for all rendering, with styling propagated through the environment by view modifiers; `Codable` for theme persistence and `Color+Codable.swift` to make SwiftUI Color round-trip; observable contexts (`KeyboardContext`, `KeyboardThemeContext`, feedback context) as the state layer, with `@MainActor` annotations on view-facing types; SF Symbols plus bundled image assets for glyphs; AudioToolbox/AVFoundation and UIFeedbackGenerator for feedback; App Groups + `FileManager.containerURL(forSecurityApplicationGroupIdentifier:)` / `UserDefaults(suiteName:)` for app-to-extension sharing. Distribution: KeyboardKit core is open source via Swift Package Manager (also on CocoaPods); KeyboardKit PRO is a commercial closed-source binary framework requiring a license key registered at launch - the theme engine, localized keyboards, emoji keyboard, autocomplete and AI features are all behind that license. Current version at time of research: 10.7.3 (July 2026).
delivery_installation_pipeline: Three channels, and the third one is where iOS gets structurally harder than Android. (1) BUNDLED-IN-CODE: predefined themes compiled into KeyboardKit Pro, marked `isPredefined: Bool` - Standard, Swifty, Minimal (each with color variations), Colorful (8), Blueprint (2), Candy Shop (2), Neon, Tron (6). (2) COMPILED CUSTOM: your own `KeyboardTheme` values written in Swift and shipped inside the app binary - the simplest and by far the most common path. (3) DYNAMIC/USER-SELECTED: because `KeyboardTheme` is Codable, an encoded theme can be persisted and swapped at runtime; `KeyboardThemeContext` exists for exactly this, exposing `currentTheme`, `currentThemeBinding` (a SwiftUI Binding for two-way UI), `settings` (auto-persisted `KeyboardThemeSettings`), and `themeChanged` (a timestamp of the last modification, used to trigger updates). KeyboardKit auto-instantiates this context at keyboard launch and injects it into the environment. WHERE ASSETS LAND: nowhere separate - the background image rides inside the theme as `imageData: Data`, so persisting a theme persists its art in one blob, and there is no assets directory to manage. FOR A CONTAINING APP TO PASS A THEME TO ITS KEYBOARD you need an App Group shared container (`UserDefaults(suiteName:)` or `FileManager.containerURL(...)`) - and that is the crux: the keyboard extension's default sandbox permits READING the shared group container but not WRITING to it, and the well-known error is 'setting preferences outside an application's container requires user-preference-write or file-write-data sandbox access'. So app -> keyboard theme delivery works, keyboard -> app write-back needs Full Access. Downloading themes from a server into the keyboard requires Full Access (no network from a sandboxed keyboard) - the usual architecture is: containing app downloads, containing app writes to the App Group, keyboard reads.
permission_store_policy_surface: The highest-friction area of the three items, and the one most likely to shape a product decision. `RequestsOpenAccess` (Info.plist, under NSExtension > NSExtensionAttributes) is the Full Access switch - Boolean, default false. With it false the keyboard is sandboxed with no network access and no write access to the shared group container. With it TRUE the keyboard gains network access, a writable shared container with its containing app, and access to Location Services, the Address Book and the Camera Roll. Practical consequence for theming: bundling themes in the binary needs NO Full Access; passing themes from the containing app to the keyboard via App Group works with read-only access, which is the default posture; but DOWNLOADING themes directly in the keyboard, or letting the keyboard write back theme selection to the shared container, requires Full Access. KeyboardKit's own docs acknowledge that some shared features - explicitly including SYNCED THEME SETTINGS and emoji recents - may require Full Access. The product cost is real: enabling Full Access triggers a scary iOS system warning ('this keyboard may be able to access all data you type, including credit card numbers') that measurably suppresses activation, so architect to avoid needing it - do the downloading in the containing app and have the keyboard read only. App Store review: downloadable theme CONTENT (images and color data) is not executable code and does not violate the rule against downloading executable code, so a theme store is viable; but user-generated theme galleries engage App Store Review Guideline 1.2 (UGC: filtering, reporting, blocking) and 5.1 privacy expectations. KeyboardKit Pro itself is a paid commercial license (subscription tiers) - a real line item, not a free dependency.
memory_performance_budget: The binding constraint on this platform, and the reason iOS theme design differs from Android at a structural level. iOS custom keyboard extensions run under a hard memory ceiling commonly cited at ~40-60MB (the widely repeated figure is ~40MB; older Apple Developer Forum reports cite crashes past ~30MB, and the exact ceiling has never been formally documented by Apple and varies by iOS version and device) - versus ~120MB for share extensions and a full app's much larger budget. Exceeding it is a hard jetsam kill, which the user experiences as the keyboard flickering away and being replaced by the system keyboard mid-typing. KeyboardKit has a documented history here: GitHub issue #179, 'Fix the emoji keyboard memory problems', covered crashes while scrolling the emoji keyboard - emoji grids being the classic memory sink - and the Pro emoji assets were subsequently VECTORIZED, which is the single most instructive mitigation in the codebase (vector glyphs instead of thousands of rasters). Theme-specific pressure points to budget for: `Keyboard.Background.imageData: Data?` holds the ENCODED image in memory as part of the theme value, and the DECODED bitmap is additional - a full-resolution phone photo decodes to tens of MB and will exceed the ceiling on its own, so any user-supplied background MUST be downsampled in the CONTAINING APP (which has a normal app budget) before being written into the theme, never decoded at source resolution in the extension. Corollary rules: pre-resize to keyboard dimensions at 2x/3x rather than storing originals; prefer color/gradient backgrounds over images where the design allows; do not hold multiple themes' image data simultaneously (a theme PICKER inside the keyboard is dangerous - build it in the containing app); and treat animation as effectively off-limits. [uncertain] - KeyboardKit publishes no explicit numeric budget, max bitmap dimension or downsampling helper that I could find; the ceiling figures above come from Apple developer-forum reports and community consensus, not from Apple documentation or KeyboardKit docs.
untrusted_theme_validation_security: Little attack surface in the framework itself, but the risk moves to YOUR pipeline. There is no zip format, so ZIP-SLIP does not apply; theme decoding is Swift `Codable`, which is type-safe and fails cleanly on malformed input (a decode throws rather than corrupting state) - stronger by default than FUTO's advisory validation, which lets a failing theme import anyway. `Keyboard.Background` and `KeyboardTheme` contain no executable content, no shader source and no script - a theme is inert data, so remote-code concerns are absent. The real hazards are ones the framework does not handle for you: (a) `imageData: Data?` is decoded by ImageIO/SwiftUI with NO size cap, so an oversized or maliciously-crafted image is both an OOM vector (fatal inside a ~40-60MB extension) and an image-parser attack surface - validate dimensions with a CGImageSource header-only pass BEFORE decoding, and enforce a hard max; (b) if you download themes, you must verify integrity yourself (signature or checksum) since nothing in KeyboardKit does; (c) untrusted JSON decoded straight into a theme should be size-capped before decoding to avoid a memory-exhaustion parse. Best practice given the App Group architecture: do all download, validation, decode-bounds checking and downsampling in the CONTAINING APP, and let the keyboard extension read only pre-validated, pre-sized data. [uncertain] - no first-party guidance on validating downloaded themes appears in the public docs.
open_source_reference_availability: Partially - and the split matters for what you can actually study. KeyboardKit CORE is fully open source at https://github.com/KeyboardKit/KeyboardKit under a permissive license, distributed via Swift Package Manager. The styling machinery you most want to read is in core: `Sources/KeyboardKit/Styling/` - `KeyboardStyle.swift` (the namespace: `public struct KeyboardStyle {}` with the note that it 'doesn't contain any protocols or any other types that are meant to be top-level types'), `Color+Codable.swift`, `Color+Keyboard.swift`, `Color+Random.swift`, `Image+Keyboard.swift`, `KeyboardAction+ButtonColor.swift` / `+ButtonFont.swift` / `+ButtonImage.swift` / `+ButtonStyle.swift` / `+ButtonText.swift`, `KeyboardFont.swift`, `KeyboardReturnKeyType+ButtonImage.swift` / `+ButtonText.swift`, `KeyboardView+StylePreview.swift`. The deprecated service protocol is preserved for reading at `Sources/KeyboardKit/_Deprecated/KeyboardStyleService.swift` alongside `KeyboardStyle+StandardStyleService.swift` - useful as a record of what the old shape covered. The THEME ENGINE ITSELF IS PRO AND CLOSED SOURCE: KeyboardKitPro ships as a binary framework, so `KeyboardTheme`'s implementation cannot be read - only its API surface via https://docs.keyboardkit.com and the public https://github.com/KeyboardKit/KeyboardKitPro/blob/master/RELEASE_NOTES.md. Net: you can study the styling PRIMITIVES and the API SHAPE of theming, but not the theme engine's internals - unlike FUTO and HeliBoard, where the whole implementation is readable.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: Developer-oriented; there is no end-user theme editor and no external/web authoring tool comparable to FUTO's. Themes are authored in SWIFT - either by calling the raw-property initializer or by taking a predefined theme and using the `KeyboardThemeCopyable` protocol / `KeyboardThemeStyleVariation` mechanism to copy-and-tweak it into a named variation (how one base yields Colorful's 8 and Tron's 6). PREVIEW support is the framework's real strength here and is genuinely better than either Android reference: `KeyboardView+StylePreview.swift` exists in core, KeyboardKit ships previewable keyboard views, and SwiftUI Previews mean a designer/developer sees the full keyboard re-render live in Xcode as they edit style values - no build-install-launch-screenshot loop of the kind the Android references require. `KeyboardThemeContext.currentThemeBinding` gives a two-way SwiftUI Binding, so building an in-app theme PICKER (or a live editor in the containing app) is straightforward. For a store/gallery: the model has `name`, `collectionName` and `author: Author?` fields anticipating a catalog, but there is NO thumbnailImage field and no thumbnail-generation helper - unlike FUTO, which makes author-supplied thumbnails a first-class manifest field with a cheap thumbnail-only load path. If you build a theme store on this, generating and caching preview thumbnails (ideally by rendering the keyboard view offscreen in the CONTAINING APP, not the extension) is work you have to add. [uncertain] - no first-party thumbnail or preview-export tooling found.
cross_platform_token_parity: No cross-platform theme format - KeyboardKit is Apple-platforms only (iOS/iPadOS primarily, with macOS/visionOS/watchOS reach in recent versions) and has no Android counterpart, so one theme definition does not render on both. Assessing portability against the Android references in this survey: PORTABLE CONCEPTS - the layered background model (backgroundColor -> gradient -> image -> overlayColor -> overlayGradient) maps almost directly onto FUTO's background+scrim stack and is the best cross-platform template of the three; role-keyed button styles (input/system/primary) map onto FUTO's normal/functional/action and HeliBoard's KEY_/FUNCTIONAL_KEY_/ACTION_KEY_ tokens with near 1:1 correspondence; corner radius, border color/size, shadow color/size, foreground/background pairs, and the callout/autocomplete token groups all have Android equivalents. INHERENTLY PLATFORM-BOUND - SwiftUI `Color` (needs the custom Codable bridge even within Swift) and `Image`; SF Symbols glyph names; `ImageContentMode` semantics; `KeyboardAction` / `KeyboardReturnKeyType` enums; the App Group + Full Access delivery model; and the absence of any dynamic-color source (Material You has no iOS analogue, so a shared format needs 'dynamic' to be an Android-only mode that degrades to a literal palette on iOS). Practical recommendation for a cross-platform product: define your own neutral token vocabulary - roles x (fg, bg, pressed, border, radius, shadow) + a layered background block + callout/toolbar/emoji groups - and write two thin adapters, rather than trying to make either platform's native format canonical.
animation_budget: Effectively none, and on iOS that is the correct answer rather than a limitation. There is NO animated theme format anywhere in the model: no Lottie, no GIF, no video, no shader/AGSL-equivalent field; `Keyboard.Background` accepts only a static `imageData: Data?` plus colors and gradients. What animation exists is functional SwiftUI micro-animation - button press states, callout appearance, the pressed overlay via `buttonPressedOverlayColor` - all frame-budget-trivial and not author-configurable through a theme. The hard reason not to want more: the ~40-60MB extension ceiling makes multi-frame assets (a GIF or video decodes to many bitmaps) hazardous, and a continuous render loop in an extension is a battery and jetsam risk with no upside for a surface the user looks at for seconds at a time. This is the sharpest contrast in the survey - FUTO runs an always-on OpenGL shader background on Android, which is simply not a safe design inside an iOS keyboard extension. OPEN / WEAKLY DOCUMENTED [uncertain]: KeyboardKit publishes no statement on animated themes as a roadmap item, no frame-rate guidance, and no pause-when-idle policy - because the feature does not exist, the question has not been answered. If a product requires animated themes on both platforms, treat iOS as the constraint that defines the ceiling: pre-rendered short loops at heavily reduced resolution, paused whenever the input view is not visible, or accept static-only on iOS.
key_takeaways_for_mochi: STATUS CORRECTION: KeyboardKit is at 10.7.3 - KeyboardStyleService was soft-deprecated in 9.8 and REMOVED in 10.0. Design against view modifiers (.keyboardButtonStyle, .keyboardViewStyle, .keyboardCalloutActions, .keyboardTheme) and never against a service subclass; 9.x tutorials showing custom services are dead.

The best single idea to copy: Keyboard.Background as an explicitly layered, Codable value - backgroundColor -> gradient -> image -> overlayColor -> overlayGradient. Making the SCRIM a first-class serializable field beats both FUTO (scrim folded into key alpha) and HeliBoard (no scrim at all).
Embedding the image as imageData: Data inside the Codable theme makes a theme genuinely self-contained - HeliBoard's shared themes silently lose their background image because they don't do this.

The 'value builder with fall-through' idiom is the right override shape: discriminate on the action, return your style, else delegate to the standard builder. Applies equally to styles and callout actions.

MEMORY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: ~40-60MB hard ceiling on the extension. Downsample user background images in the CONTAINING APP, never decode at source resolution in the keyboard; build the theme PICKER in the app, not the extension; vectorize emoji assets (KeyboardKit's own issue #179 fix).

ARCHITECT AROUND FULL ACCESS: app downloads + validates + writes to the App Group, keyboard reads only. Downloading in the extension or writing back from it needs RequestsOpenAccess = true, whose scary system warning measurably suppresses activation.

GAPS to fill yourself: no normalized crop rect (only a fit/fill content mode - add FUTO's fractional cropping); no thumbnail field or preview-generation helper (FUTO's author-supplied thumbnailImage is the model); no schema version (stamp your own into the persisted envelope); no contrast validation.
KeyboardKit Pro is a paid commercial license and the theme engine is closed-source binary - you can study the API shape and the open-source styling primitives, but not the engine.
